"Rises 1 in 10" is a **gradient**: one unit of height for every ten units measured along
the slope.
**Step 1 — read the gradient.** A rise of 1 in 10 means
height/length = **1/10**
**Step 2 — apply it to the given length.**
height = (1/10) x 5
= **0·5 m** ✓
**What the gradient means geometrically.** It is the **sine** of the angle of
inclination, since
sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse = height/length ✓
so here sin θ = 0·1, giving θ = **5·74°** - a gentle slope, the sort used for ramps.
**A check on the base.** The horizontal distance covered is
√(5² − 0·5²) = √24·75 = **4·97 m** ✓ barely less than the 5 m slope, as a shallow incline
requires.
**The engineering convention.** Road and railway gradients are quoted this way -
"1 in 10", "1 in 50" - and because such slopes are shallow, it hardly matters whether the
10 is measured along the slope or along the horizontal ✓ Here the question says "length
of the inclined plane", which is the slope itself, so the division is direct.
**Why the answer is not 0·1 m.** That would be the rise for a slope of length **1 m** ✗
The question gives 5 m, so the rise is five times as great ✓
**Reading the other distractors.** **0·25 m** ✗ is the rise for a 2·5 m slope.
**1·0 m** ✗ is the rise for a 10 m slope, or a gradient of 1 in 5 ✓ Scaling the ratio
by the actual length is the whole of the calculation.
∴ 0·5 m.

The remark is one of the most quoted lines in physics, and it belongs to **Albert
Einstein**.
**The statement.** "The most incomprehensible thing about the world is that it is
comprehensible" ✓ Einstein wrote it in 1936, in an essay on the method of physics.
**What he meant by it.** There is no logical guarantee that nature should be describable
by a handful of mathematical laws ✓ It might have been arbitrary, lawless or endlessly
complicated. That a few equations - Newton's, Maxwell's, Einstein's own - should capture
so much of it is, as he saw it, the genuine wonder.
**Why it matters to a physics student.** The whole enterprise of physics rests on this
unproven faith: that the universe is **orderly**, that the same laws hold here and in a
distant galaxy, and that experiment can reveal them ✓ Every chapter of a physics book
takes that for granted.
**The others, and what they are known for.**
**Niels Bohr** - the quantum model of the atom, and the complementarity principle; he is
remembered for "anyone who is not shocked by quantum theory has not understood it"
**Ernest Rutherford** - the nuclear atom, from the gold-foil experiment
**Marie Curie** - the discovery of polonium and radium, and the first person to win two
Nobel Prizes ✓
None of them is the author of this particular remark.
**A related Einstein line.** "Subtle is the Lord, but malicious He is not" - the same
thought, that nature is hard to read but not perverse ✓
∴ Einstein.

"Science is the art of the soluble" points at how science **chooses its questions**, and
at the economy of its answers.
**The phrase.** It is the title of a 1967 book by the biologist **Peter Medawar** ✓ His
point was that science advances by attacking problems that are actually **solvable** with
the tools at hand, not by brooding on questions beyond reach.
**What it implies about physical laws.** A problem becomes soluble when it can be reduced
to a few general principles ✓ So the claim being tested is that **different phenomena can
be explained in terms of only a few fundamental laws** - the unifying economy that makes
science workable.
**The evidence for that economy.** Newton's law of gravitation explains the fall of an
apple, the orbit of the Moon and the tides - three unrelated-looking phenomena from one
equation ✓ Maxwell's four equations cover electricity, magnetism and light together. The
whole of thermodynamics rests on a handful of laws.
**Why the other statements are wrong.**
"Every great physical theory ends as a **dogma**" ✗ - the opposite of the scientific
method, which holds every theory open to revision by experiment. Newtonian mechanics was
not preserved as dogma; it was superseded where it failed.
"Every physical theory starts as a **hearsay**" ✗ - theories begin from observation and
hypothesis, not rumour ✓
"None of the above" ✗ is unnecessary once the first statement is seen to fit.
**The deeper point.** Solubility is why physics is taught as a small set of laws rather
than an encyclopaedia of separate facts ✓ The art lies in finding the question that those
few laws can answer.
∴ different phenomena can be explained in terms of only a few fundamental laws.

All three named factors have held back scientific progress, and they reinforce one
another.
**Lack of education.** Science needs a wide base of trained people - teachers,
technicians, engineers, researchers ✓ Where literacy is low, that base is thin, and
scientific talent goes undiscovered however abundant it may be.
**Poverty.** Research needs laboratories, instruments, libraries and sustained funding ✓
A poor economy spends on immediate needs first, and basic science, whose returns are slow
and uncertain, is the easiest item to postpone.
**Uncontrolled population.** Rapid growth stretches the same resources across more
people ✓ Spending per student and per researcher falls, and the pressure for immediate
food, housing and employment crowds out long-term investment in knowledge.
**Why they are not independent.** Poverty limits education; limited education weakens the
case for family planning; a growing population deepens poverty ✓ The three form a cycle,
which is precisely why the question offers "all the above" rather than asking you to
pick the single worst.
**The counter-evidence.** Where these barriers have been eased, progress has followed -
India's work in space technology, nuclear power, information technology and
pharmaceuticals shows what a trained, funded scientific community achieves ✓ The barriers
are circumstantial, not inherent.
**Why no single option can be right.** Each of the three is genuinely a hindrance, so
selecting any one of them would mean denying the other two ✓ When every listed factor is
individually correct, "all the above" is the only consistent answer.
∴ all the above.

The statement is **true**, and its truth illustrates how physics establishes the
existence of things it cannot see.
**Why no one has seen an electron.** Seeing requires **visible light** to scatter off an
object and enter the eye. Visible wavelengths are about **500 nm**, while an electron is
smaller than 10⁻¹⁸ m - at least a billion times smaller ✓ Light simply passes by; there
is nothing to reflect an image.
**The deeper obstacle.** Even an ideal microscope cannot resolve detail finer than about
half the wavelength used ✓ To "see" an electron one would need radiation of a wavelength
smaller than the electron, whose photons would carry such enormous energy that they would
blast it away - a limitation quantum mechanics makes fundamental, not merely technical.
**How we know electrons exist anyway.** Through their **effects**, every one of which is
measurable:
**Thomson's cathode-ray experiment** measured e/m from the deflection of the beam
**Millikan's oil-drop experiment** measured the charge e itself
**cloud and bubble chambers** show the **tracks** electrons leave in a vapour
**electric currents, thermionic emission and the photoelectric effect** all behave exactly
as a stream of such particles would ✓
**What this teaches about physics.** Much of what science accepts as real is known
**indirectly** - atoms, nuclei, quarks, neutrinos, black holes ✓ Evidence need not be
visual to be conclusive; a consistent web of independent measurements is stronger than a
glance.
**Why "false" and "cannot say" are wrong.** "False" ✗ would claim someone has seen one,
which no experiment supports. "Cannot say" ✗ ducks a question that is settled: the
statement is plainly true, and we also know **why** it is true ✓
∴ true.

Each of the three named developments has transformed how science and technology are
done, so all of them belong in the answer.
**Superconducting materials.** A superconductor carries current with **zero resistance**
✓ This makes possible the powerful magnets used in **MRI scanners**, in particle
accelerators such as the LHC, and in magnetically levitated trains - and promises
lossless power transmission.
**Superfast computers.** Computation has become a third pillar of science alongside
theory and experiment ✓ Weather forecasting, protein folding, climate models, the
simulation of galaxies and the analysis of accelerator data are all impossible without
it.
**Robots.** They work where humans cannot - inside nuclear reactors, on the sea bed, on
the surface of Mars, and on the production line with a precision no hand can match ✓
Laboratory robots also run experiments continuously and reproducibly.
**Why all three together.** Each one amplifies the others ✓ Superconducting magnets
generate data that only supercomputers can process; robots gather it; the design of
better superconductors is itself done by simulation. The revolution is in their
combination, not in any one of them.
**The common thread.** All three extend human capability past a natural limit - **of
resistance, of calculation, of physical reach** ✓ That is what makes them revolutionary
rather than merely useful.
**Why no single option can be right.** Each development is genuinely part of the present
scientific revolution, so choosing one would mean excluding two that are equally valid ✓
∴ all the above.

Three of the four are neutral or beneficial technologies; one is an application that is
both harmful and illegal.
**Prenatal sex determination.** Used to identify the sex of a foetus, it has led to
widespread **female foeticide** and a badly skewed sex ratio ✓ India's
**Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act, 1994** makes
disclosing the sex of a foetus a criminal offence for this reason. It is the clear
example of science misused.
**Why the other three are good uses.**
**computers** - they drive research, education, medicine, banking and communication ✓
**artificial satellites** - weather forecasting, cyclone warnings, telecommunications,
remote sensing, navigation and disaster management all depend on them, and in India they
carry tele-education and tele-medicine to remote villages ✓
**radio and television** - mass education, news, warnings and entertainment, reaching
people no other medium reaches ✓
**The point the question makes.** Science itself is **neutral**; it provides capability,
and the use made of it is a human choice ✓ The same ultrasound scanner that saves lives
by monitoring a pregnancy can be abused to end one.
**Note on the underlying technology.** Ultrasound imaging is not the villain - it is
indispensable in obstetrics ✓ What is prohibited is the specific use of it to determine
and disclose sex, which is why the option names that application rather than the
instrument.
**Reading the question.** It asks which is **not** a good use, so the answer is the one
harmful item among three benign ones ✓ Misreading the negative is the only real trap.
∴ prenatal sex determination.

The remark about beauty in equations is **Paul Dirac's**, and it is characteristic of how
he worked.
**The quotation.** "It is more important to have beauty in one's equations than to have
them fit experiment" ✓ Dirac wrote it in 1963, looking back on the development of quantum
mechanics.
**What he meant.** Experiments can be wrong, and early measurements often are ✓ A theory
with real mathematical elegance - symmetry, economy, inevitability - has, in his
experience, usually turned out to be right in the end, even when the data of the day
seemed against it. He was arguing against abandoning a beautiful theory at the first
awkward measurement.
**His own vindication.** The **Dirac equation** of 1928 combined quantum mechanics with
special relativity. Its mathematics demanded negative-energy solutions, which looked like
an embarrassment ✓ Dirac trusted the equation, interpreted them as a new particle, and
the **positron** was found in 1932 - the first antiparticle, predicted from the beauty of
an equation rather than from any experiment. He shared the 1933 Nobel Prize for it.
**The caution that goes with it.** The remark is not a licence to ignore evidence ✓
Elegance is a guide to **where to look**, while experiment remains the final judge - a
beautiful theory that is definitively contradicted is still wrong.
**The others, and their famous lines.**
**Niels Bohr** - "anyone who is not shocked by quantum theory has not understood it"
**Isaac Newton** - "if I have seen further, it is by standing on the shoulders of giants"
**C. V. Raman** - Nobel laureate for the Raman effect, the scattering of light ✓
None of these is the author of the remark in question.
∴ PAM Dirac.
